items.prose: Nim: take 1, 2 or 3; whoever takes the last stick wins. The pile has 30 sticks and it is your move.
items.question: How many do you take?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave a multiple of 4.

items.prose: A variant lets each player take 1 to 4 sticks; the last stick still wins. The losing piles are now the multiples of 5.
items.question: From 23 sticks, how many do you take?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave a multiple of 5.

byKey.left: That is the pile you leave. The question asks how many you take.

items.prose: A max root has three min children with leaves (4, 10), (7, 2) and (6, 9).
items.question: What is the root's value?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Back up each min node first.

byKey.helps: Your opponent never lets you reach 10.
byKey.worst: You choose the branch; take the best minimum.

explain.text: The min nodes are 4, 2 and 6, so the root is 6.

items.prose: Alpha-beta, left to right, on a max root with three min children: (6, 8, 7), (3, 9, 5), (7, 4, 9).
items.question: How many leaves are read?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Stop a min node once it is at or below the best so far.

byKey.all: Pruning skips leaves once a branch cannot beat 6.
byKey.seven: In the last branch, 4 is already below 6, so 9 is skipped.

explain.text: The first branch is read in full (worth 6). The second stops at 3, the third at 4. That is $3 + 1 + 2 = 6$ leaves.

items.question: Alpha-beta and minimax are run on the same game. What can differ?

options.text: Only the number of nodes visited
Both the value and the nodes

options.why: Pruning saves work: 18,297 nodes against 549,946 in tic-tac-toe.

explain.text: Every cut skips a line that cannot change the choice above it, so the value is unchanged.

items.question: Which count is the number of different tic-tac-toe boards that can arise in play?

options.why: That is every way to fill nine cells with X, O or blank, legal or not.
That is the number of complete games.
That is the number of nodes in the full game tree.

explain.text: Of the $3^9 = 19{,}683$ fillings, 5,478 are reachable; the tree visits them 549,946 times over 255,168 games.

items.prose: A child has won 5 of 10 playouts; its parent has 50 visits; $c = \sqrt 2$.
items.question: What is its UCT score? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the average and the bonus.

byKey.nosq: You left out the square root.

explain.text: The average is 0.5 and the bonus $\sqrt2 \times \sqrt{0.3912} = 0.8845$, so the score is 1.3845.

items.prose: MCTS has finished its iterations. Root child P has 3 visits and average 0.9; child Q has 70 visits and average 0.8.
items.question: Which move should it play?

options.why: Three playouts is a small sample.
The search already spent its budget where it mattered.

explain.text: UCT kept choosing Q because it kept doing well; P's high average rests on three games.

items.prose: Self-play Nim: after your move, the opponent's best value at the new pile is 0.25.
items.question: What target updates your move's value?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Negate the opponent's best value.

byKey.sign: Their good position is bad for you.

explain.text: Zero-sum: your target is minus their best, $-0.25$.

items.question: Which pairing of an AlphaZero network with what it replaces in plain MCTS is right?

options.why: The policy network steers selection with move priors.
Visits are still counted and choose the move.

feedback.correct: The value network scores positions instead of playing them out.

explain.text: The policy network sets priors for selection; the value network replaces simulation (reading: Silver et al. 2018).
